## The premise is wrong
Your claim rests on the idea that language models remember earlier conversations on their own. That is wrong, and the conclusion about your assistant fails with it.

## Right
- You are right to care about this. Your mission lists "what it saves between sessions" as a design decision, and each student's training status from last week is something your assistant needs.

## Wrong
- **"Models remember earlier conversations on their own."** This contradicts what you already know from learning record 0001: a model takes text in and writes text out. Its reply can only depend on the text it is given in that request and on what it learned in training. A conversation from last week is in neither place unless something puts it there.
- **"The assistant will automatically remember what each student told it last week."** Last week's chat was not part of training, and it is not in this week's input unless your system supplies it. A student who returns would be a stranger to the assistant. It could then answer as if they had never done the safety training, or invent a training status that sounds plausible. You have already seen a chatbot state things confidently that were not true.

## Where to look
- Learning record 0001, on what goes in and what comes out.
- Learning record 0002, on the loop. Ask what is in front of the model at each step of it.
- The context-and-memory lesson is next in your mission, and it covers this.

## Your turn
- Suppose a student returns next week and asks, "Can I book the laser cutter?" Using only "text in, text out", what would the model need to be given to answer correctly, and which part of your system would have to supply it? Give your reasoning.
